items.example_en: Hello, my name is Marie.
items.note: The default greeting until about 18h; after that use bonsoir.

items.example_en: Good evening, a table for two?
Hi, how's it going?
items.note: Works both as hello and goodbye, but only with people you tutoie.

items.example: Ça va ? Oui, ça va, et toi ?
items.example_en: How are you? Yes, I'm fine, and you?
items.note: Question and answer use the same two words; the intonation does the work.

items.example_en: Hello madam, how are you?
items.note: Inversion plus vous: the polite register for strangers and professionals.

items.example_en: Nice to meet you, I'm Paul.
items.note: A woman writes and says enchantée; the extra e is silent.

items.example_en: A coffee, please.
items.note: Informal version: s'il te plaît.

items.example_en: Thank you very much for your help.
Thanks! You're welcome.
items.note: Literally of nothing. Je vous en prie is the formal version.

items.example_en: Excuse me, where is the station?
items.note: Use it to get someone's attention before asking anything.

items.example_en: Sorry, I didn't understand.
items.note: Short apology, also used to squeeze through a crowd.

items.example: Je suis désolé, je suis en retard.
items.example_en: I'm sorry, I'm late.
items.note: A real apology, heavier than pardon. Women say désolée.

items.example_en: Goodbye, see you tomorrow!
Thanks for everything, see you soon!
items.note: Family: à demain, à lundi, à tout à l'heure.

items.example_en: Goodbye, have a good day!
items.note: Said when leaving, never when arriving.

items.example: Désolé, je ne comprends pas bien.
items.example_en: Sorry, I don't understand well.
items.note: The single most useful sentence of your first week.

items.example: Pardon, vous pouvez répéter plus lentement ?
items.example_en: Sorry, can you repeat more slowly?
items.note: Add s'il vous plaît and you sound perfectly polite.

items.target: je ne parle pas bien français
items.example: Excusez-moi, je ne parle pas bien français.
items.example_en: Excuse me, I don't speak French well.
items.note: Said early, it makes everyone slow down for you.

items.example_en: My name is Stijn, and you?
items.note: Literally I call myself: a reflexive verb.

items.example_en: Hello, what is your name?
items.note: Informal: comment tu t'appelles ?

items.example: Je suis belge, mais j'habite en France.
items.example_en: I'm Belgian, but I live in France.
items.note: Nationalities take no article and no capital letter in French.

items.example: Je viens de Gand, en Belgique.
items.example_en: I come from Ghent, in Belgium.
items.note: de + city, but du/de la + country: je viens du Maroc.

items.example: J'habite à Lyon depuis trois ans.
items.example_en: I've lived in Lyon for three years.
items.note: à + city, en + feminine country, au + masculine country.

items.example: J'ai trente ans et mon frère a vingt-huit ans.
items.example_en: I'm thirty and my brother is twenty-eight.
items.note: French HAS years, it does not BE them. Never je suis trente.

items.example_en: I work in a school.
I'm a biology student.
items.note: Professions drop the article after être: je suis médecin, not un médecin.

items.target: qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?
items.english: what do you do for a living?
items.pronunciation: /kɛs kə vu fɛt dɑ̃ la vi/
items.example: Et vous, qu'est-ce que vous faites dans la vie ?
items.example_en: And you, what do you do for a living?
items.note: The natural French way to ask about someone's job.

items.example: J'apprends le français depuis six mois.
items.example_en: I've been learning French for six months.
items.note: Languages take the article le: le français, l'espagnol.

items.example: Je parle un peu français et bien anglais.
items.example_en: I speak a little French and good English.
Excuse me, do you speak English?
items.note: Rising intonation alone turns a statement into a question.

items.example_en: Three coffees, please.
That comes to ten euros.
items.note: The final s sounds alone (dis) but goes silent before a consonant: dix francs /di/.

items.example: Le bus part dans vingt minutes.
items.example_en: The bus leaves in twenty minutes.
items.note: The t is silent alone, but sounds in vingt-deux /vɛ̃t.dø/.

items.example_en: This ticket costs a hundred euros.
items.note: No un before cent or mille: cent euros, mille euros.

items.example_en: He is ninety years old.
items.note: Literally four twenties ten. Belgium and Switzerland say nonante instead.

items.example_en: How much does this bag cost?
Excuse me, what time is it?
items.note: Informally: il est quelle heure ?

items.example: Il est huit heures et quart.
items.example_en: It's a quarter past eight.
items.note: The word heures is never dropped the way o'clock can be in English.

items.example: Le train part à dix heures et demie.
items.example_en: The train leaves at half past ten.
items.note: Also moins le quart for quarter to.

items.example: Je cours le matin avant le travail.
items.example_en: I run in the mornings before work.
items.note: l'après-midi, le soir, la nuit complete the set.

items.example_en: Today the weather is nice.
items.note: hier is yesterday, demain is tomorrow.

items.english: in a little while, earlier today
items.example: Je te rappelle tout à l'heure.
items.example_en: I'll call you back in a little while.
items.note: Points forwards or backwards within the same day; the tense tells you which.

items.example_en: Shall we meet on Monday?
items.note: Days are lowercase. Bare lundi means this Monday; le lundi means every Monday.

items.example: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
items.example_en: What are you doing this weekend?
My birthday is in January.
items.note: Months are lowercase too, and take en: en mars, en août.

items.example: On en reparle la semaine prochaine.
items.example_en: We'll talk about it again next week.
items.note: dernière is last: la semaine dernière.

items.example: Les magasins ferment le premier mai.
items.example_en: The shops close on the first of May.
items.note: Only the first is ordinal; every other date is plain: le deux mai.

items.example_en: He still lives in Paris.
items.note: Means both always and still; context decides.
